q-kadikoy.angle_note: the place and Chalcedon; the market streets have their own card in the larder

old_cards.name: Kadıköy
old_cards.teaser: The shore an oracle called blind. It has the star now.
old_cards.body: Megaran settlers founded Chalcedon on this headland seventeen years before Byzantium went up across the water — the oracle called them blind for choosing the wrong shore. Mehmed II gave the farmland to Hızır Bey, Istanbul's first Ottoman judge, and Chalcedon became kadı-köy , the judge's village. The joke has aged badly. Araf's star, Çiya's field-recording kitchen and the deepest Turkish wine list in the city are all on this side now, and the European side crosses over for dinner. Asian shore · vapur from Eminönü, Karaköy and Beşiktaş, about 20 minutes

old_cards.name: Moda
old_cards.teaser: Wooden villas built by three communities, and the pier that outlived them.
old_cards.body: The headland below Kadıköy, laid out in the late nineteenth century when Greek, Armenian and Levantine families built wooden summer houses down the lanes to the water. Their churches — Hagia Triada among them — still hold services; their congregations are a fraction of what they were. The Vedat Tek ferry pier of about 1917 has been restored as a book café and public library, and the coast path around the point is the best free hour on the Asian side. Walk it westward into the sunset. Moda, Kadıköy · 15 minutes on foot from Kadıköy pier, or the heritage tram loop

old_cards.name: Yeldeğirmeni
old_cards.teaser: Windmills, railway workers, and the first apartment blocks on this shore.
old_cards.body: Named for the flour mills that once ground for the palace, and settled since the fifteenth century by Armenians, Greeks and Jews — a handful of families remain. It was the first quarter in Kadıköy to build apartment blocks instead of wooden houses, and several of the originals still stand on their streets. A mural programme covered the gable walls a decade ago; the coffee and the quieter rooms followed. Coffee Manifesto holds this end of the district. Go in the morning. Kadıköy, between the ferry pier and Haydarpaşa

old_cards.name: Üsküdar
old_cards.teaser: The gold city, and where the caravans set out for Mecca.
old_cards.body: Megaran settlers again, this time calling it Chrysopolis, the golden city. Ottoman Üsküdar was the terminus of the Anatolian caravan routes and, for much of the Ottoman period, the point at which the Surre caravan left the mainland carrying the sultan's gifts to Mecca; the regular caravan ended in 1915. That made it Muslim, settled and sober while the rest of the city was mixed and licensed — which is why the lokantas here are superb and the meyhanes essentially absent. Asian shore · ferries from Eminönü and Beşiktaş

q-kuzguncuk.angle_note: the place and its three houses of prayer; the street walk is in Walks: one clause

old_cards.name: Kuzguncuk
old_cards.teaser: A synagogue, an Armenian church and a mosque, all on one street.
old_cards.body: Once a largely Jewish village on the Asian shore. Along İcadiye Caddesi stand a mosque, the Bet Yaakov synagogue of 1878, an Armenian church and Greek Orthodox ones. Almost none of those congregations still live here. It is the physical proof of everything this guide argues, and it takes ten minutes to walk. Asian shore, one stop north of Üsküdar · İcadiye Caddesi runs up from the water

q-pera.group: Pera and the hill above it

old_cards.group: Pera and the hill above it
old_cards.name: Beyoğlu / Pera
old_cards.teaser: The avenue was called Grand Rue de Péra, and it was not Turkish.
old_cards.body: Pera is Greek for beyond — the quarter across the Golden Horn from the old city. Foreigners won the right to buy property here in 1867 and built the Grand Rue de Péra with it: arcades, apartment houses and hotels in every style the century could supply. The Cité de Péra of 1876 became the Çiçek Pasajı, its elegant shops turned into rough meyhanes with barrels for tables. İstiklal Caddesi runs Taksim to Tünel · Asmalımescit and Nevizade at its lower end

q-cihangir.group: Pera and the hill above it

old_cards.group: Pera and the hill above it
old_cards.name: Cihangir
old_cards.teaser: A dead prince's mosque, then the writers, now the small serious rooms.
old_cards.body: Named for the mosque Sinan built in 1559 for Şehzade Cihangir, Süleyman's son, dead at twenty-two; the present building is an 1889 replacement after repeated fires and earthquakes. The slope below Taksim became the writers-and-cats quarter in the 1990s and has held that register better than most gentrified districts manage. Two rooms from this guide sit here: Casius, cooking Antakya food and carrying a 2026 Bib Gourmand, and Østre, the oyster and raw bar that opened this year. Beyoğlu, on the slope between Taksim and Fındıklı

q-nisantasi.group: Pera and the hill above it

old_cards.group: Pera and the hill above it
old_cards.name: Nişantaşı
old_cards.teaser: Named for the stones that recorded how far a sultan's arrow flew.
old_cards.body: A nişan taşı is an inscribed stele recording a record shot: Selim III's here dates from 1790–91, Mahmud II's from 1811. Mahmud II then encouraged settlement and the archery ground became the city's grandest residential grid. It is not a cooking quarter. It is a drinking and listening one — Lips for natural wine, and June and Dama in Teşvikiye next door, the second a café that turns hi-fi bar after dark. Şişli · runs into Teşvikiye and Harbiye

old_cards.name: Karaköy and Galata
old_cards.teaser: A Genoese city-state with its own walls, now the cruise front.
old_cards.body: Galata was a colony of the Republic of Genoa from 1267 to 1453 — walled, self-governing, and topped by the tower it finished in 1348. Five centuries later the banker Abraham Salomon Camondo cut his baroque staircase down to Bankalar Caddesi so he could walk from his house to his bank. Galataport reopened this waterfront to the public in 2021. Neolokal holds a star above it; the roof bars hold the view. Beyoğlu, at the mouth of the Golden Horn · Kamondo stairs off Bankalar Caddesi

q-balat-fener.angle_note: one card for the two neighbouring quarters; the walks hold the routes

old_cards.name: Balat
old_cards.teaser: Five centuries of Jewish Istanbul, sold now as a colour photograph.
old_cards.body: The name is probably from palation , palace, for the Blachernae ruins on the hill above. Sephardic and Romaniote families lived here for five centuries; the Ahrida synagogue, founded in the 1430s by Jews from Ohrid, is one of the oldest in the city and still in use. Agora Meyhanesi, which dates itself to 1890, is the reason to be here after dark. The painted staircases draw a queue by mid-morning, so do the lanes first and the photograph never. Fatih, on the Golden Horn · Ahrida synagogue visits by prior arrangement

old_cards.name: Fener
old_cards.teaser: The first throne of Orthodoxy, and a red school on the hill.
old_cards.body: Phanar, the lighthouse, named the quarter and then the Phanariots — the Greek families who supplied the Ottoman state its dragomans, its interpreters and its Danubian princes. The Ecumenical Patriarchate is still here, and above it stands the Phanar Greek Orthodox College, the Red Castle, built 1881–83 by the architect Konstantinos Dimadis at a recorded cost of 17,210 Ottoman gold pounds. The school itself opened in 1454, the year after the conquest. It has outlasted the community it was built to teach. Fatih, on the Golden Horn immediately north of Balat

q-arnavutkoy.group: Up the strait — the Bosphorus villages

old_cards.group: Up the strait — the Bosphorus villages
old_cards.name: Arnavutköy
old_cards.teaser: The great current, an Albanian name, and a strawberry that lost its fields.
old_cards.body: Byzantine Mega Revma, the great current, for the water that runs fastest along this bank. Mehmed II resettled Albanians here in 1468 and the Turkish name followed, but the village stayed heavily Greek into the twentieth century, with Armenian and Jewish families beside them. It grew the Ottoman strawberry — small, less sweet than the modern berry, intensely scented — on forty hectares of hillside that are now streets. The bay-windowed wooden yalı are the best surviving row on the European shore. Tam Ocakbaşı cooks here. Beşiktaş, European shore · the waterside walk north to Bebek is about 3 km

q-bebek.group: Up the strait — the Bosphorus villages

old_cards.group: Up the strait — the Bosphorus villages
old_cards.name: Bebek
old_cards.teaser: A palace demoted to a consulate when the capital left.
old_cards.body: The name means baby, and the bay is the calmest water on the European shore, which is why the yalı here belong to people who can afford calm. The white art nouveau pile on the front was built 1899–1901 for Emine Valide Pasha, mother of the last Khedive of Egypt; it became the Egyptian embassy and was later downgraded to a consulate once the capital moved to Ankara. The whole city's demotion, in one building. Beşiktaş, European shore · walk in from Arnavutköy along the water

q-tarabya.group: Up the strait — the Bosphorus villages

old_cards.group: Up the strait — the Bosphorus villages
old_cards.name: Tarabya
old_cards.teaser: Poison, renamed cure, then rented to ambassadors.
old_cards.body: Byzantine Pharmakia — poison, after the Medea legend — until it was renamed Therapeia, the cure, for its springs; tradition credits Archbishop Atticus, some time between 406 and 425. It became the summer address of the embassies. Abdülhamid II gave the German one its plot in 1880; the residence went up between 1885 and 1887 and has run since 2011 as an artists' residency. The bay below is a fish-restaurant row, and Arogan, with Burak Zafer cooking, opened above it this year. Sarıyer, European shore · the far end of the Bosphorus road, north of Yeniköy

w-kadikoy-ferry.angle_note: one home for the ferry as the best room in the city

old_cards.name: Eminönü to Kadıköy
old_cards.teaser: The commute that happens to be the best twenty minutes in the city.
old_cards.body: The line traces back to the Şirket-i Hayriye of 1851, the Ottoman empire's first joint-stock company; the boats today are run by Şehir Hatları, municipal since 2006 and working 32 lines from 53 piers. Take the open deck, order tea from the tray that never spills, and watch the old city separate from Galata as you pull out. It is transport rather than a tour, which is exactly why it is worth doing. Eminönü pier, Fatih · Şehir Hatları · pay with İstanbulkart, no ticket queue

old_cards.name: The vapur — Şehir Hatları ferry
old_cards.teaser: The best room in Istanbul moves, and costs almost nothing.
old_cards.body: Şirket-i Hayriye began running boats across the strait in 1851, and until the first Bosphorus bridge opened in 1973 the water was the only way over. Şehir Hatları still works 30 boats on 32 lines between 53 piers, and carried 40 million passengers in 2023. Tea comes round in tulip glasses on a tray that never spills; gulls track the stern for thrown simit. Twenty minutes, both shores lit, no table and no plug — and that is the entire point. Piers at Eminönü, Karaköy, Beşiktaş and Kadıköy · roughly 20–25 minutes across

old_cards.name: Karaköy or Eminönü to Üsküdar
old_cards.teaser: The shortest hop to Asia — take it back westward with the sun going down.
old_cards.body: Üsküdar was Chrysopolis, founded by colonists from Megara in the seventh century BC, and for centuries the point at which Asia began: the caravan roads east and the pilgrim road to Mecca started from this shore. The Maiden's Tower stands offshore — a Byzantine tower of 1110 on a rock the Athenians had already used as a customs post, rebuilt repeatedly since; what you see is Ottoman. Sinan's Mihrimah Sultan mosque sits above the pier and his small Şemsi Paşa mosque almost in the water. Cross back westward at dusk and the European skyline lights up in front of you. Üsküdar pier · frequent all day · Şemsi Paşa mosque is a few minutes south along the water

old_cards.name: The Golden Horn line — Üsküdar to Eyüpsultan
old_cards.tag: ~50 min end to end · hop off
old_cards.teaser: One boat, nine piers, and the door of every walk in the next group.
old_cards.body: The Haliç line runs Üsküdar, Karaköy, Kasımpaşa, Fener, Balat, Hasköy, Ayvansaray, Sütlüce, Eyüpsultan — which is to say it stops at the door of every walk in the next group. The Golden Horn is 7.5 km long and was an industrial sewer within living memory; the clean-up through the 1980s and 1990s is the reason you can now sit on deck and enjoy it. Ride to the top, walk, and come back by boat. Board at Üsküdar or Karaköy · alight at Fener or Balat · same İstanbulkart fare

old_cards.name: Arnavutköy to Bebek
old_cards.teaser: Painted timber houses on the water, then a bay full of boats.
old_cards.body: Arnavutköy means Albanian village — by tradition Mehmed II settled Albanians here after 1453. The painted timber houses standing straight out of the water, late nineteenth and early twentieth century with Art Nouveau fronts, line the shore road. Walk north along it into Bebek, past the Egyptian consulate, raised 1899 to 1901 for the mother of Egypt's last khedive, and stop at the bay. START Arnavutköy pier, north along the shore road · free · flat throughout, no shade at midday

old_cards.name: Kuzguncuk's one street
old_cards.teaser: A mosque, a synagogue and a church on the same short road.
old_cards.body: İcadiye Caddesi runs a few hundred metres up from the water, and along it stand a mosque, the Bet Yaakov synagogue — conventionally dated 1878 and probably older — an Armenian church and Greek Orthodox ones. Sephardic Jews settled here after the expulsions from Spain; the oldest Jewish gravestone in the neighbourhood is dated 1562. The community thinned after 1948 and emptied fast after the 1955 pogrom, replaced by migrants from the Black Sea coast. One street, the whole argument. START Kuzguncuk pier, or a short bus north from Üsküdar · free · residential — keep the volume down

old_cards.name: Moda and the Kadıköy sea walk
old_cards.teaser: The flat seafront the Asian side actually uses, pointed at the sunset.
old_cards.body: Moda became fashionable from the 1870s as a summer quarter for Greek, Armenian and Levantine families, which is why Greek Orthodox, Anglican and Catholic churches and the 1870 Lycée Saint-Joseph still stand among the apartment blocks. The pier building dates from 1917 and was restored in 2022. Walk out to Moda Burnu, sit on the grass with everyone else and watch the sun drop behind the Historic Peninsula. The nostalgia tram loops back into Kadıköy. START Kadıköy pier, south along the shore · free · Kadıköy–Moda nostalgia tram runs the loop back

w-fener.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
w-fener.angle_note: the iron church is on the Fener shore: one walk

old_cards.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
old_cards.name: Fener — the Patriarchate and the Red Castle
old_cards.teaser: Orthodoxy's senior see, on a back street, behind an iron gate.
old_cards.body: The Ecumenical Patriarchate has sat here since about 1600, and the Phanariot Greeks of this quarter supplied the Ottoman state its dragomans and, between 1711 and 1821, the governors of Wallachia and Moldavia. Above it rises the vast red-brick Phanar Greek Orthodox College, which now has almost no pupils, and that is the plainest measure of what happened here. Nearby, St Mary of the Mongols is the only Byzantine church in the city that has never stopped being a Greek Orthodox place of worship; the firmans of Mehmed II and Bayezid II granting it to the Greek community still hang there. Fener pier on the Haliç line · St George's Cathedral free, modest dress · the college is not open to visitors

old_cards.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
old_cards.name: The iron church of St Stephen
old_cards.teaser: A church cast in Vienna, shipped down the Danube, bolted together here.
old_cards.body: The Bulgarians broke from the Greek Patriarchate in 1870 and wanted a church of their own. The Ottoman Armenian architect Hovsep Aznavur drew it on an iron frame because the ground here is soft; the Austrian firm R. Ph. Waagner cast some 500 tonnes of parts in Vienna between 1893 and 1896 and shipped them down the Danube and across the Black Sea. Consecrated 8 September 1898, restored 2011 to 2018. A whole church made of metal. Mürselpaşa Caddesi, on the shore road between Fener and Balat piers · free

w-balat.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier

old_cards.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
old_cards.name: Balat — Ahrida and the Jewish quarter
old_cards.teaser: Eighteen synagogues once; three still working, one with a bimah shaped like a prow.
old_cards.body: Bayezid II opened the city to Jews fleeing the Spanish Inquisition after 1492 and Balat became the centre of Istanbul's Jewish life, with eighteen synagogues at its height. Ahrida was founded in the fifteenth century by Jews from Ohrid; its wooden bimah is built in the shape of a boat's prow, and Sabbatai Zevi prayed here — the only Istanbul synagogue where he did. He had proclaimed himself the Messiah at Smyrna at Rosh Hashanah in 1665, and on reaching Constantinople in February 1666 he was arrested on the order of the grand vizier Köprülüzade Fazıl Ahmed Pasha. Three synagogues still work. Balat is now overwhelmingly Muslim, and in the 2020s heavily gentrified. Kürkçü Çeşme Sokak, Balat · synagogue visits only by prior arrangement through the Jewish community · steep streets

w-eyup.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
w-eyup.angle_note: Pierre Loti's tea garden has its own card in the rooms to linger: one clause

old_cards.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
old_cards.name: Eyüpsultan and the hill above it
old_cards.teaser: A pilgrimage mosque, a cemetery up the slope, and a cable car to the view.
old_cards.body: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, a companion of the Prophet, died during the Arab siege of Constantinople in the 670s. His tomb was declared rediscovered after 1453, and the mosque raised over it became the place where each new sultan was girded with the Sword of Osman. It is a working pilgrimage site, so dress for it and avoid Friday midday. Above, the cemetery climbs to the Pierre Loti café, named for the French novelist and reached by cable car. Eyüpsultan pier at the head of the Golden Horn · mosque free, modest dress · teleferik up to the café

old_cards.name: Büyükada
old_cards.teaser: The largest of the Princes' Islands, and the one where the horses were taken away.
old_cards.body: Horse-drawn phaetons were the only transport on the island until 2020, when they were phased out after a serious equine disease and replaced by battery-powered electric vehicles that work like taxi cabs; islanders have since resisted the arrival of buses in the pedestrianised zone. The building everyone photographs, the Greek Orthodox orphanage on the Hristos ridge, went up in 1898 to a design by Alexander Vallaury and is believed to be the largest wooden structure in Europe and the second largest in the world — it took in children until 1964, has stood empty since, and a restoration was announced in 2021. Trotsky spent the first four years of his exile here, April 1929 to July 1933, in the Yanaros mansion, now a ruin. Şehir Hatları has run the islands 24 hours a day since 2019. The honest catch: the two buildings people travel for are both shut, the quayside kitchens are priced for day-trippers, and on a summer weekend the return-ferry queue is the memory you take home. The tell — Climb Yücetepe, the island's 202-metre high point, to the Greek Orthodox monastery of Aya Yorgi — probably founded in the tenth century, though what stands is mid-18th to 19th century — where the café on the grounds serves wine, chips and sausage sandwiches. The pilgrimage falls on 23 April, St George's Day, and the hill is mobbed for it. On the water, the 1911 Splendid Palace and its twin domes is the landmark. Adalar — 25 min by fast ferry or 40 min by regular ferry from Kabataş; also served from Eminönü, Beşiktaş, Kadıköy, Bostancı and Maltepe · Year-round; ferries run 24/7. Go on a weekday out of high summer.

old_cards.name: Büyükada by ferry
old_cards.teaser: Five and a half square kilometres with no engine noise in them.
old_cards.body: The Byzantines exiled inconvenient royals here, which is where the name comes from. A 1912 census counted roughly 10,250 Greeks to 670 Turks across the nine islands; this was a Greek, Armenian and Jewish summer world and it is not one now. Private cars are still banned. The horse phaetons have gone too: an outbreak of glanders among the horses finished them, and an Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality council decision of 16 January 2020 ended the phaeton era for good, with electric vehicles taking over the same summer. Ferries from Kabataş, Beşiktaş and Eminönü (about 90 min) or Bostancı and Kadıköy (about 45) · bicycles for hire at the pier

o-st-george.angle_note: the climb and the orphanage on the way: one home for the orphanage

old_cards.name: The Monastery of St George
old_cards.teaser: A steep climb that Muslims and Christians make together on the saint's day.
old_cards.body: Aya Yorgi sits at the island's highest point, 203 metres up. A chapel of 1751 stood here; the present cut-stone church was begun in 1905 and finished in 1909. The origin story — icons buried during a medieval sack and rediscovered after a shepherd's dream — is the standard one for a Greek shrine. What is not standard is the crowd: on 23 April, St George's day, thousands climb the path, and a great many of them are Muslim. Yücetepe, Büyükada · walk up from Birlik Meydanı, roughly 40 min · steep, no shade, carry water

old_cards.name: The Prinkipo Orphanage
old_cards.teaser: Europe's largest wooden building, twenty thousand square metres of it, empty since 1964.
old_cards.body: Alexandre Vallaury designed it in 1898 for the Wagons-Lits company as the Prinkipo Palace, a hotel and casino for Orient Express passengers. Abdülhamid II refused the licence; a Greek banker's wife bought it and gave it to the Patriarchate, and it opened as an orphanage on 21 May 1903. Turkish authorities forced it shut on 21 April 1964, the year of the expulsions. Confiscated in 1997, returned after Strasbourg ruled against Turkey. In the pines above Büyükada, on the way up to Aya Yorgi · closed and unsafe — look from outside only

old_cards.name: Prinkipo Greek Orthodox Orphanage
old_cards.teaser: Europe's largest wooden building, shut by the state in 1964 and empty since.
old_cards.body: Alexandre Vallaury — the architect of the Ottoman Bank — built it in 1898 for the Wagons-Lits company, which ran the Orient Express, as a hotel and casino. Abdülhamid II refused the operating permit. In 1903 Eleni Zarifi bought it and gave it to the Ecumenical Patriarchate, which ran it as an orphanage for Greek children until Turkish authorities forced it shut on 21 April 1964. Twenty thousand square metres of timber have stood open to the weather since. Title was returned in 2012; a restoration partnership was signed in June 2026. Büyükada, Princes' Islands · uphill from the pier; the building is closed and derelict, so this is an exterior

old_cards.name: Heybeliada
old_cards.teaser: The quiet island next door, with a seminary at the top of it that has been closed since 1971 and is still a diplomatic file.
old_cards.body: The Theological School of Halki was founded in 1844 inside the Hagia Triada monastery and trained clergy for the Ecumenical Patriarchate until 1971, when the Constitutional Court struck down parts of Turkey's private higher-education law; it has never reopened and remains closed to the public. The Naval High School overlooking the jetty was founded in 1773 and holds the Byzantine church of the Kamariotissa and the relocated grave of Edward Barton, Elizabeth I's ambassador to the Porte. The island is 2.35 square kilometres with 4,424 residents at the 2022 count, rising to around 30,000 in high summer. Phaetons were banned here in 2020 along with the rest of the islands and replaced by electric vehicles; private cars are still prohibited, with only ambulances, fire tenders and police allowed. The catch: both buildings that give the island its meaning are institutional and shut, so come for the pine ridge and the swimming, not for a tour. The tell — Hire a bike at the jetty and ride the ring road under the pines — the island is small enough to circle in an hour and quiet enough that you hear it. Aya Triada on Ümit Tepesi, restored by Patriarch Photios I in the ninth century, is the roofline you look up at from the road, and looking up is as close as you get. Adalar — the call before Büyükada on ferries from Kabataş, Eminönü, Beşiktaş, Kadıköy, Bostancı and Maltepe · Year-round; the island empties out of season, which is the point.

old_cards.name: Heybeliada and the closed seminary
old_cards.teaser: The school that trained a thousand priests, closed by a law about colleges.
old_cards.body: The Theological School of Halki opened on 1 October 1844 on the hill above Heybeliada and turned out close to a thousand priests, bishops and patriarchs. In 1971 Turkish legislation banning private higher education closed it, and it has taken no student since — though Ankara and the Patriarchate announced in 2026 that it will reopen. American presidents and the EU have pressed for that for decades. The monastery keeps the building, the library and the view. Get off one island early. Hill above Heybeliada pier · the grounds are not a public museum — access is occasional and by arrangement · quieter than Büyükada

old_cards.name: Anadolu Kavağı & Yoros Kalesi
old_cards.teaser: The last village before the Black Sea, and the much-conquered castle on the hill above it.
old_cards.body: Yoros stands above the confluence of the Bosphorus and the Black Sea and changed hands more often than almost any fort in Turkey: the Ottomans took it in 1305 and held it again from 1391 to 1414, the Genoese held it for the forty years to 1454 — which is why locals still call it the Genoese Castle — and Mehmed II refortified it after 1453. It was excavated between 2018 and 2021 and is open to the public again, though the ground immediately around it remains a military area and is closed; the site sits on the UNESCO tentative list. The village below is tiny, 1,517 residents at the 2022 count plus the garrisons, and keeps a mosque commissioned by Ali Pasha of Midilli in 1593 and a fountain of 1785. The catch: the entire quay is calibrated to a boat that arrives and leaves, the layover is fixed, and missing the return sailing puts you on a long bus down the Asian shore. The tell — Fish on the quay — pick it off the ice and agree the price before it is cooked, because this is a captive-audience waterfront and the bill is where day-trippers get caught. Then walk up to the castle: a steep twenty minutes from the pier, with the Third Bosphorus Bridge on one side and open Black Sea on the other. Beykoz — terminus of Şehir Hatları's twice-daily Long Bosphorus Tour from Eminönü, calling at Sarıyer and Rumeli Kavağı on the way up · The long tour runs twice daily; confirm the timetable with Şehir Hatları on the day of travel.

old_cards.group: Out of the city for a day
old_cards.name: The long ferry to Anadolu Kavağı
old_cards.teaser: The whole strait end to end, on a commuter boat with a lunch stop.
old_cards.body: The long Şehir Hatları service runs from Eminönü to Anadolu Kavağı at the northern mouth of the Bosphorus, calling at Sarıyer and Rumeli Kavağı, and holds at the top long enough for lunch before turning back. Above the village stands Yoros Castle, fortified under the late Byzantines, Ottoman from 1391, lost to Genoa in 1414 for forty years — which is why everyone calls it the Genoese castle — then refortified by Mehmed II. Departs Eminönü Boğaz İskelesi · twice daily · the village is a row of fish restaurants and prices there are tourist-grade

o-rumeli-kavagi.angle_note: Balıkçı Kahraman is a table card: name it, do not retell

old_cards.name: Rumeli Kavağı
old_cards.teaser: Get off one stop early, on the European bank, where the fish is the same water and the audience is not.
old_cards.body: This is the northernmost settlement on the European side of the strait, and the majority of its 3,560 residents (2024 count) descend from Eastern Black Sea migration — which is what ends up on the plate. The village is known locally for exactly three things: fish, mussels and figs. A Byzantine fortress once stood here and was demolished on Mehmed II's order; excavation has also turned up traces of a Byzantine temple and harbour works beneath the settlement. The catch: nearly every cruise passenger stays aboard for the castle across the water, so there are fewer kitchens open here and no schedule built around visitors — check before you commit an evening to it. The tell — Midye — mussels — and whatever came in that morning, cooked plainly and without ceremony. If you want open sea rather than strait, the Rumeli Feneri lighthouse and the fishing hamlet of Garipçe are a short ride further north. Sarıyer — the last European call on the Long Bosphorus Tour, one stop before Anadolu Kavağı · Best in the fish months, autumn through early spring.

old_cards.name: Hıdiv Kasrı
old_cards.teaser: An Art Nouveau summer palace built in 1907 for the Khedive of Egypt, on a bluff over the Bosphorus.
old_cards.body: The Khedive of Egypt — the Ottoman viceroy of a province richer than most of the empire — built his holiday house on this headland in 1907, and it is one of the very few grand houses around Istanbul where you get inside the rooms rather than photographing a façade, because the building now trades as a restaurant and café inside its own public park. The catch is twofold. It is a working hospitality business in a historic shell, so go for the terrace and the grounds rather than for the cooking. And I could not reach a live source to confirm current opening hours in August 2026 — treat the visit as unconfirmed and telephone before you make the climb, which is a genuine hill from the waterline and unpleasant in high summer. The tell — The park and the terrace over the strait, best in the morning before the light goes flat. A drink is what buys you the interior, so order one and walk the rooms rather than booking a full dinner. Beykoz — Çubuklu, on the Asian shore; ferry to Kanlıca then a climb, or bus and taxi from Beykoz · Not verified for 2026 — call ahead before travelling. Heads up — Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-15 — call ahead.

old_cards.group: Forest, coast and the far shore
old_cards.name: Belgrad Ormanı
old_cards.teaser: Five and a half thousand hectares of forest with Istanbul's Ottoman waterworks buried in it.
old_cards.body: The forest takes its name from the Serbs deported here after Süleyman the Magnificent's 1521 siege of Belgrade, settled to maintain the water supply. Two Ottoman systems ran through it: the older Kırkçeşme network, rebuilt by Mimar Sinan under Süleyman, and the eighteenth-century Taksim system, whose Mahmud I aqueduct went up at Bahçeköy in 1732. What you actually walk to are the bents — the dammed Ottoman reservoirs — on a 6.5-kilometre marked track that starts at Neşet Suyu, with seven picnic grounds of which Büyük Bent is the busiest. The catch, and it sends people to the wrong district: Mağlova, Sinan's masterpiece and the aqueduct in every photograph, is not in this forest. It stands in the Alibey valley near Cebeci in Sultangazi, 257 metres long and 35 metres high on two tiers, built between 1555 and 1562 — and roughly a quarter of it is drowned by the Alibeyköy reservoir, so the full span is visible only when the water level drops. The tell — Start at Bahçeköy, walk the Neşet Suyu track to Büyük Bent, and detour to the Atatürk Arboretum — over 2,000 plant species, about twenty minutes on foot from the village. Bring the food with you: this is picnic country, not restaurant country, and Bahçeköy is where you buy it before you go in. Sarıyer and Eyüp — 5,524 hectares; Bahçeköy is the hub and is well served by city buses, roughly an hour from Beyoğlu depending on traffic · Autumn for colour, spring for water. Picnic areas fill on summer weekends.

old_cards.group: Out of the city for a day
old_cards.name: Belgrad Forest
old_cards.teaser: The oak forest north of the city, and the waterworks that supplied Ottoman Istanbul.
old_cards.body: The name is literal: Süleyman deported thousands of Serbs from Belgrade to the capital in 1521, and the village they were settled in named the forest. Two Ottoman systems ran through it — the sixteenth-century Kırkçeşme network upgraded by Sinan, and the eighteenth-century Taksim one — and their dams and aqueducts, among them the Maglova aqueduct and the Mahmud I arch of 1732, still stand among the sessile oaks. Some 5,500 hectares, with a 6.5 km running loop. Bahçeköy, Sarıyer · about an hour from the centre by road · Büyük Bent is the busiest gate · go early, it fills at weekends

old_cards.name: Polonezköy
old_cards.teaser: A Polish village in the Beykoz forest, founded in 1842 by an exiled prince and still holding on to the language.
old_cards.body: Prince Adam Jerzy Czartoryski established the settlement in 1842 for Poles displaced by the failed November Uprising and named it Adampol, a Polish rendering of the Turkish Adamköy; it started with twelve inhabitants and grew through later waves of emigration. Many went home after Poland regained independence in 1918, and those who stayed took Turkish citizenship in 1938. At the 2022 count the village had 346 residents, of whom roughly ninety speak fluent Polish — so what survives is a community held together by memory, a church and a summer festival of Polish folk bands, not a living Polish town. The catch: at weekends Istanbul drives out here en masse and the single approach road becomes a queue. Go midweek or do not go. The tell — The Memorial House of Zofia Rizi, which keeps the photographs, books, documents and original interiors of a village house; the church of Our Lady of Częstochowa; and the Polish cemetery, where 92 graves have been restored. The pensions along the road serve the long forest-edge breakfast that is the actual reason most Istanbullus make the drive. Beykoz — about 30 km from the historic centre; realistically a drive or a taxi, there is no useful public transport · Weekdays. The summer festival is the one weekend worth the traffic.

old_cards.group: Forest, coast and the far shore
old_cards.name: Şile & Ağva
old_cards.teaser: Istanbul's Black Sea coast: an 1859 French-built lighthouse, a crimped cotton cloth, and a village between two rivers.
old_cards.body: The Şile lighthouse was built in 1859 by French engineers for Sultan Abdülmecid I and lit in 1860 — a 19-metre octagonal tower carrying eight 925-millimetre catadioptric lenses with a range of 20 nautical miles, electrified since 1968 and open to visitors as a historic site. The town also gives its name to Şile bezi, the crimped cotton cloth sold across Istanbul's bazaars, with a fair for it each summer; the fourteenth-century Genoese castle on Ocaklı Ada was renovated in 2015 to widespread mockery for looking like a cartoon. Ağva sits between the Göksu and the Yeşilçay — the name means 'between the rivers' — with a 2.5-kilometre beach and small boats running up the Göksu, and its 2,150 residents swell to around 15,000 in season. The catch here is not crowds, it is water: the undercurrents on this coast are strong enough that people drown at these beaches every year. Swim between flags or not at all. The tell — Walk into the lighthouse — one of very few in Turkey you can enter. Buy the Şile bezi in Şile rather than off a Sultanahmet stall. And in Ağva take the river rather than the sea: the pensions face the Göksu, which is the argument for staying the night instead of driving 97 km twice in a day. Şile district — Şile is the northernmost point of Istanbul province; Ağva is 38 km further east, about 97 km from the centre · June to September for swimming; the coast road jams every summer weekend.
